title: Young black musicians cannot play the blues
summary: Ridgley laments that young New Orleans black musicians in 1986 don't know blues or read, so he hires white players.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Yeah, well you were talking about, we're on reel number two with Tommy Ridgely on,
86. So we were talking about dramas.

Yeah, well I was talking about the present drummer that I have in my present band today, and I stated just a minute ago that I have been associated with better musicians in all of my days, and I'm talking about from way back with doing the Earl Palmer era with David Tholomew, Ernest MacLange, Salvador Doucette, see these people are musicians, there ain't no F and A's about it. Okay, that's a caliber musician I have dealt with. All the way up my band, the original Untouchables, Larry Marino, Charlie Burbank, and Dalton Russo, Buddy Williams, all these people could play. And today, and I'm saying this, and I guess people probably read about this, because I know Ted's going to write it. Okay, now what I'm saying is here in New Orleans, June 1986, a lot of the young black musicians are missing, they call it, they're not playing up to par. They enter another bag of things, they don't know nothing about playing that black heritage music. They couldn't play a decent blues, and I'm talking about the majority of them. They couldn't play a decent blues if you just, if I just walk up and say play some blues in blow blow key. They're going to ask me, first of all, a lot of stupid questions like, how many changes? What you mean how many changes? Play some blues. You know, see, because this is the way I feel about it. But this is what have happened to the young black musicians. And you talk to all people who are in the music business my age, and a few years younger and stuff, they're going to tell you the same thing. The young black musicians cannot play. If I want to get some blues played today here in New Orleans, I've got to go find some white musicians.

And this is the truth, boy, and we talk about it, but you know, there's nothing we can do because the young black musicians into this, and that, to me, that ain't no music. It's a bunch of bullcups. And it's getting on my nerves. And like I said, I'm having problems right now finding black musicians to play. When I went there to answer the phone just now, I was talking to the guy. He's going to call a white bass player that he may call before I finish his sentence. A white bass player to get him to play with me who can play and read and know where I'm coming from. See, because that's what it's all about. Where I'm coming from, the young black musicians don't know. It's pitiful. See, when I go to clubs where a young black band is playing, the reason they won't call me is because they can't play behind me. Sure. I go in the white club.
Play everything. It's kind of pitiful. Well, can we stay on the rhythm thing?
